article.title: Raising the Mary Rose

items.sentence_raw: On 19 July 1545, English and French fleets were engaged in a sea battle off the coast of southern England in the area of water called the Solent, between Portsmouth and the Isle of Wight.
Among the English vessels was a warship by the name of Mary Rose.
Built in Portsmouth some 35 years earlier, she had had a long and successful fighting career, and was a favourite of King Henry VIII.

Accounts of what happened to the ship vary: while witnesses agree that she was not hit by the French, some maintain that she was outdated, overladen and sailing too low in the water, others that she was mishandled by undisciplined crew.
items.explain: Q1: The passage says *'Accounts of what happened to the ship vary'* — this means people tell different stories about the sinking. **'Vary'** means **'differ'**, which directly matches the question's idea of **'some doubt'**. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: What is undisputed, however, is that the Mary Rose sank into the Solent that day, taking at least 500 men with her.
After the battle, attempts were made to recover the ship, but these failed.
The Mary Rose came to rest on the seabed, lying on her starboard (right) side at an angle of approximately 60 degrees.
The hull (the body of the ship) acted as a trap for the sand and mud carried by Solent currents.
As a result, the starboard side filled rapidly, leaving the exposed port (left) side to be eroded by marine organisms and mechanical degradation.
Because of the way the ship sank, nearly all of the starboard half survived intact.
items.explain: Q3: The passage says *'nearly all of the starboard half survived intact'* — **'starboard'** means the **right side** of the ship. **'Survived intact'** means it stayed **undamaged**. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the entire site became covered with a layer of hard grey clay, which minimised further erosion.
Then, on 16 June 1836, some fishermen in the Solent found that their equipment was caught on an underwater obstruction, which turned out to be the Mary Rose.
items.explain: Q8: The passage says *'on 16 June 1836, some fishermen... found that their equipment was caught on an underwater obstruction, which turned out to be the Mary Rose'* — they found it **by accident**, not by searching. **'By chance'** means **'by accident'**. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Diver John Deane happened to be exploring another sunken ship nearby, and the fishermen approached him, asking him to free their gear.
Deane dived down, and found the equipment caught on a timber protruding slightly from the seabed.
Exploring further, he uncovered several other timbers and a bronze gun.
Deane continued diving on the site intermittently until 1840, recovering several more guns, two bows, various timbers, part of a pump and various other small finds.
items.explain: Q6: The passage says Deane *'continued diving on the site intermittently until 1840'* — **'until 1840'** means his exploration **stopped** in that year. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: The Mary Rose then faded into obscurity for another hundred years.
But in 1965, military historian and amateur diver Alexander McKee, in conjunction with the British Sub-Aqua Club, initiated a project called 'Solent Ships'.
items.explain: Q5: The passage says *'in 1965... Alexander McKee... initiated a project called 'Solent Ships''* — **'initiated a project'** means he **'launched a search'**. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: While on paper this was a plan to examine a number of known wrecks in the Solent, what McKee really hoped for was to find the Mary Rose.
Ordinary search techniques proved unsatisfactory, so McKee entered into collaboration with Harold E. Edgerton, professor of electrical engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
In 1967, Edgerton's side-scan sonar systems revealed a large, unusually shaped object, which McKee believed was the Mary Rose.
Further excavations revealed stray pieces of timber and an iron gun.
But the climax to the operation came when, on 5 May 1971, part of the ship's frame was uncovered.
McKee and his team now knew for certain that they had found the wreck, but were as yet unaware that it also housed a treasure trove of beautifully preserved artefacts.
items.explain: Q4: The passage says McKee's team *'were as yet unaware that it also housed a treasure trove of beautifully preserved artefacts'* — **'unaware'** means they **did not know**. But the question says McKee **'knew'** it would contain valuable objects. These are opposites, so the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: Interest in the project grew, and in 1979, The Mary Rose Trust was formed, with Prince Charles as its President and Dr Margaret Rule its Archaeological Director.
The decision whether or not to salvage the wreck was not an easy one, although an excavation in 1978 had shown that it might be possible to raise the hull.
While the original aim was to raise the hull if at all feasible, the operation was not given the go-ahead until January 1982, when all the necessary information was available.
items.explain: Q7: The passage says *'the operation was not given the go-ahead until January 1982'* — **'given the go-ahead'** means it was **'agreed'** to raise the hull. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: An important factor in trying to salvage the Mary Rose was that the remaining hull was an open shell.
This led to an important decision being taken: namely to carry out the lifting operation in three very distinct stages.
The hull was attached to a lifting frame via a network of bolts and lifting wires.
items.explain: Q9: The passage says *'The hull was attached to a lifting frame via a network of bolts and lifting wires'* — the **'lifting frame'** is attached to the hull by wires. So the answer is **lifting frame**.

items.sentence_raw: The problem of the hull being sucked back downwards into the mud was overcome by using 12 hydraulic jacks.
items.explain: Q10: The passage says *'The problem of the hull being sucked back downwards into the mud was overcome by using 12 hydraulic jacks'* — the **'hydraulic jacks'** stopped the hull from being sucked into the mud. So the answer is **hydraulic jacks**.

items.sentence_raw: These raised it a few centimetres over a period of several days, as the lifting frame rose slowly up its four legs.
It was only when the hull was hanging freely from the lifting frame, clear of the seabed and the suction effect of the surrounding mud, that the salvage operation progressed to the second stage.
In this stage, the lifting frame was fixed to a hook attached to a crane, and the hull was lifted completely clear of the seabed and transferred undewater into the lifting cradle.
items.explain: Q12: The passage says the hull was *'transferred undewater into the lifting cradle'* — the hull is lowered into the **'lifting cradle'**. So the answer is **lifting cradle**.

items.sentence_raw: This required precise positioning to locate the legs into the 'stabbing guides' of the lifting cradle.
items.explain: Q11: The passage says *'locate the legs into the 'stabbing guides' of the lifting cradle'* — the legs are placed into the **'stabbing guides'**. So the answer is **stabbing guides**.

items.sentence_raw: The lifting cradle was designed to fit the hull using archaeological survey drawings, and was fitted with air bags to provide additional cushioning for the hull's delicate timber framework.
items.explain: Q13: The passage says the cradle *'was fitted with air bags to provide additional cushioning for the hull's delicate timber framework'* — **'cushioning'** means **'extra protection'**. So the answer is **air bags**.

items.sentence_raw: The third and final stage was to lift the entire structure into the air, by which time the hull was also supported from below.
Finally, on 11 October 1982, millions of people around the world held their breath as the timber skeleton of the Mary Rose was lifted clear of the water, ready to be returned home to Portsmouth.

subtitles: How a sixteenth-century warship was recovered from the seabed

orphan_explain_map.2: Q2: The passage only talks about the *Mary Rose* sinking — it says *'the Mary Rose sank into the Solent that day'*. It never mentions any other ships sinking in that battle. Since we don't know if other ships sank or not, the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
